warmup.q: 100 coroutines on a Dispatchers.Default.limitedParallelism(1) view each run val b = balance; val c = fx.convert(1); balance = b + c, where fx.convert is a suspend call to the FX service. Each credit adds 1. What is balance at the end?
options: Exactly 100, because only one coroutine runs at a time on the view
Usually far less than 100, because the coroutines interleave at fx.convert
Exactly 100, but only if fx.convert doesn't suspend for long
The code fails, because a one-thread view rejects concurrent coroutines
warmup.why: A one-thread view runs one coroutine at a time only between suspension points. When a credit suspends in fx.convert, the thread is free and the next credit reads the same old balance. When they resume, each writes its own b + c over the others. The KDoc's own heading for this is "limitedParallelism(1) is not a mutex!".

sections.h: Coroutines on Default race like threads, and the same tools fix them
sections.html:
Coroutines on Dispatchers.Default run on several threads at once, so shared mutable state needs the same care as in the threads track. counter++ from 100 coroutines loses updates. @Volatile doesn't help, and the coroutines guide says so in as many words: "volatiles are of no help". A volatile write is atomic and visible, but read, add and write are still three steps.

Pick the tool by the shape of the update.

  • One value, changed in one atomic step: an atomic. AtomicLong.incrementAndGet(), AtomicReference.updateAndGet, or MutableStateFlow.update { } from lesson 8 of this track. They never suspend and never block. Kotlin 2.1.20 also added common atomics such as AtomicInt in kotlin.concurrent.atomics, as an experimental API; on the JVM the java.util.concurrent.atomic classes do the same job.
  • Several steps that must happen together: a Mutex.
  • State that one coroutine owns: confinement. Keep the map inside one coroutine and send it requests through a channel (lesson 9 of this track).

Mutex is the coroutine lock:

Java
// Java equivalent: a ReentrantLock around the same read-modify-write
private final ReentrantLock lock = new ReentrantLock();

void credit(String account, long cents) {
    lock.lock();
    try { balances.put(account, balances.getOrDefault(account, 0L) + cents); }
    finally { lock.unlock(); }
}
Kotlin
private val mutex = Mutex()

suspend fun credit(account: String, cents: Long) = mutex.withLock {
    balances[account] = (balances[account] ?: 0L) + cents
}

withLock takes the lock, runs the block in a try, and releases the lock in finally, the same idiom as Java's. The difference is what waiting costs. Mutex.lock() suspends the coroutine, so a credit waiting for the lock holds no thread. The KDoc gives the Mutex the memory semantics of a synchronized block, and makes it fair: waiters get the lock in the order they asked.

Two warnings come with it. A Mutex is not reentrant. Its KDoc gives it two states, locked and unlocked, and unless you pass an owner token for debugging it keeps no record of who holds it, so a second lock can't tell its own holder from anyone else. (ReentrantLock records the owning thread, which would not work here: a coroutine may resume on another thread.) A coroutine that holds it and calls withLock again suspends forever, waiting for itself, so a transfer that calls credit while holding the lock deadlocks. Take the lock once, at the top. And the guide's measurements show that fine-grained locking, a lock or a dispatcher switch around every tiny increment, is slow. Lock around a meaningful unit of work, or use an atomic for a single number.

try.title: Count a million payments five ways
steps: Read SharedCounter.kt. 100 coroutines on Default each count 10,000 payments. Predict which counters reach 1,000,000, and which is slowest.
Run the Java twin, which uses 8 threads and a ReentrantLock.

code.title: SharedCounter.kt
code.html: package workbench.coroutines.l10 import kotlinx.coroutines.CoroutineScope import kotlinx.coroutines.Dispatchers import kotlinx.coroutines.coroutineScope import kotlinx.coroutines.launch import kotlinx.coroutines.runBlocking import kotlinx.coroutines.sync.Mutex import kotlinx.coroutines.sync.withLock import kotlinx.coroutines.withContext import java.util.concurrent.atomic.AtomicLong import kotlin.system.measureTimeMillis private var plain = 0L @Volatile private var volatileCount = 0L /** 100 coroutines on Dispatchers.Default each count 10,000 captured payments. */ suspend fun count(label: String, increment: suspend CoroutineScope.() -> Unit, read: () -> Long) { val ms = measureTimeMillis { coroutineScope { repeat(100) { launch(Dispatchers.Default) { repeat(10_000) { increment() } } } } } println("%-28s %,9d of 1,000,000 in %4d ms".format(label, read(), ms)) } fun main() = runBlocking { count("plain var", { plain++ }, { plain }) count("@Volatile var", { volatileCount++ }, { volatileCount }) val atomic = AtomicLong() count("AtomicLong", { atomic.incrementAndGet() }, { atomic.get() }) val mutex = Mutex() var guarded = 0L count("Mutex.withLock", { mutex.withLock { guarded++ } }, { guarded }) val confined = Dispatchers.Default.limitedParallelism(1) var onOneThread = 0L count("withContext(limited(1))", { withContext(confined) { onOneThread++ } }, { onOneThread }) }

alt.title: SharedCounterJava.java
alt.html: // Java equivalent of SharedCounter.kt: the same counter on 8 platform threads. Coroutines on // Dispatchers.Default run in parallel, so they race exactly like threads do. package workbench.coroutines.l10; import java.util.concurrent.ExecutorService; import java.util.concurrent.Executors; import java.util.concurrent.atomic.AtomicLong; import java.util.concurrent.locks.ReentrantLock; import java.util.function.LongSupplier; public class SharedCounterJava { static long plain = 0; static volatile long volatileCount = 0; static long guarded = 0; static void count(String label, Runnable increment, LongSupplier read) { long t0 = System.nanoTime(); try (ExecutorService pool = Executors.newFixedThreadPool(8)) { for (int t = 0; t < 100; t++) pool.submit(() -> { for (int i = 0; i < 10_000; i++) increment.run(); }); } System.out.printf("%-28s %,9d of 1,000,000 in %4d ms%n", label, read.getAsLong(), (System.nanoTime() - t0) / 1_000_000); } public static void main(String[] args) { count("plain field", () -> plain++, () -> plain); count("volatile field", () -> volatileCount++, () -> volatileCount); AtomicLong atomic = new AtomicLong(); count("AtomicLong", atomic::incrementAndGet, atomic::get); ReentrantLock lock = new ReentrantLock(); count("ReentrantLock", () -> { lock.lock(); try { guarded++; } finally { lock.unlock(); } }, () -> guarded); } }

try.expect: The plain and @Volatile counters come out short, by a different amount each run. AtomicLong, Mutex.withLock and the one-thread view all reach exactly 1,000,000. AtomicLong is fastest by far; the Mutex and the withContext switch for every increment take about a second, because each increment pays for a lock or a dispatch. The Java twin shows the same split, with ReentrantLock much cheaper than a Mutex here because these threads never suspend.

sections.h: A one-thread view is not a mutex
sections.html:
A view such as Dispatchers.Default.limitedParallelism(1) runs at most one of its coroutines at a time. That looks like a lock, and the KDoc has a heading of its own to say it isn't one: "limitedParallelism(1) is not a mutex!"

The view guarantees that code between suspension points runs one coroutine at a time, with a happens-before edge from each to the next, so counter++ on it is safe. But the moment a coroutine suspends, the view's thread is free and the next coroutine runs. Any sequence that suspends in the middle is open to interleaving:

Java
// Java equivalent: one thread, but an async step in the middle
CompletableFuture.supplyAsync(() -> balances.getOrDefault(account, 0L), oneThread)
    .thenCombine(fx.toEurCentsAsync(amount, currency), Long::sum)        // another credit runs meanwhile
    .thenAcceptAsync(after -> balances.put(account, after), oneThread);  // writes over the other credit
Kotlin
withContext(oneAtATime) {
    val before = balances[account] ?: 0L
    val cents = fx.toEurCents(amount, currency)    // suspends: another credit runs here
    balances[account] = before + cents             // writes over the other credit
}

Play it out in the simulator: two credits, one thread, and a suspension in the middle of each. (The simulator lets you switch after any line. On the real view a switch can only happen at the suspending line, and that is enough to lose a credit.)

There are two fixes. Move the suspension out of the critical part: convert first, then do the read and the write with nothing that suspends between them. On a one-thread view that is now safe, because nothing else can run in the middle. Or hold a Mutex across the whole sequence, which keeps other credits out even while the holder is suspended. The first is faster, because the conversions overlap. Use the second when the suspending call really must sit inside, for example a ledger check whose answer must not go stale before you write.

The general rule is the one you learned for threads. A critical section is safe only if nothing else can run in the middle of it. For coroutines, "in the middle" means any suspension point, including the ones hidden inside functions you call.

sim.title: Two credits on limitedParallelism(1)
sim.intro: Both credits run on a one-thread view, so only one runs at a time. But each one gives the thread away when it suspends in fx.toEurCents. You are the scheduler: click a credit to run its next line. Can you end with balance = 100 after two credits of 100?

steps.code: val cents = fx.toEurCents(1, "EUR")   // suspends: the thread is free
val cents = fx.toEurCents(1, "EUR")   // suspends: the thread is free

goal.say: Lost credit. Both read 0 before either wrote. One coroutine at a time between suspensions is not one credit at a time.

try.title: Interleave three credits, then lock them
steps: Read NotAMutex.kt. Predict the order of the read and write lines for the one-thread view, then for the Mutex.
Look at the last part: why does the nested withLock time out instead of returning inner?
Run the Java twin, where a single-thread executor interleaves the same way and ReentrantLock happily locks twice.

code.title: NotAMutex.kt
code.html: package workbench.coroutines.l10 import kotlinx.coroutines.Dispatchers import kotlinx.coroutines.delay import kotlinx.coroutines.joinAll import kotlinx.coroutines.launch import kotlinx.coroutines.runBlocking import kotlinx.coroutines.sync.Mutex import kotlinx.coroutines.sync.withLock import kotlinx.coroutines.withContext import kotlinx.coroutines.withTimeoutOrNull fun main() = runBlocking { val oneAtATime = Dispatchers.Default.limitedParallelism(1) println("limitedParallelism(1):") List(3) { i -> launch(oneAtATime) { println(" credit $i: read balance") delay(20) // the FX call suspends: the single thread is free for someone else println(" credit $i: write balance") } }.joinAll() println("Mutex.withLock:") val mutex = Mutex() List(3) { i -> launch(Dispatchers.Default) { mutex.withLock { println(" credit $i: read balance") delay(20) // still suspends, but nobody else can enter the lock println(" credit $i: write balance") } } }.joinAll() println("Mutex is not reentrant:") val nested = withTimeoutOrNull(500) { mutex.withLock { withContext(Dispatchers.Default) { mutex.withLock { "inner" } } // the same coroutine tree locks again } } println(" nested withLock -> ${nested ?: "timed out after 500 ms: it waits for itself"}") }

alt.title: NotAMutexJava.java
alt.html: // Java equivalent of NotAMutex.kt: a single-thread executor runs one task at a time, but an // async step (a CompletableFuture chain) lets the next task start before the first one has // written. A ReentrantLock held across the whole read-call-write keeps them apart, and unlike // Kotlin's Mutex it IS reentrant. package workbench.coroutines.l10; import java.util.List; import java.util.concurrent.CompletableFuture; import java.util.concurrent.ExecutorService; import java.util.concurrent.Executors; import java.util.concurrent.TimeUnit; import java.util.concurrent.locks.ReentrantLock; import java.util.stream.IntStream; public class NotAMutexJava { public static void main(String[] args) throws Exception { ExecutorService oneThread = Executors.newSingleThreadExecutor(); System.out.println("single-thread executor:"); List<CompletableFuture<Void>> credits = IntStream.range(0, 3).mapToObj(i -> CompletableFuture.runAsync(() -> System.out.println(" credit " + i + ": read balance"), oneThread) // the FX call is async: the thread is free while it waits .thenCompose(v -> CompletableFuture.runAsync(() -> { }, CompletableFuture.delayedExecutor(20, TimeUnit.MILLISECONDS))) .thenRunAsync(() -> System.out.println(" credit " + i + ": write balance"), oneThread) ).toList(); CompletableFuture.allOf(credits.toArray(CompletableFuture[]::new)).join(); oneThread.shutdown(); System.out.println("ReentrantLock around the whole credit:"); ReentrantLock lock = new ReentrantLock(); try (ExecutorService pool = Executors.newFixedThreadPool(3)) { for (int i = 0; i < 3; i++) { int n = i; pool.submit(() -> { lock.lock(); try { System.out.println(" credit " + n + ": read balance"); Thread.sleep(20); // a blocking FX call, inside the lock System.out.println(" credit " + n + ": write balance"); } catch (InterruptedException e) { Thread.currentThread().interrupt(); } finally { lock.unlock(); } }); } } System.out.println("ReentrantLock is reentrant:"); lock.lock(); try { lock.lock(); // the same thread takes it again try { System.out.println(" nested lock -> inner (hold count " + lock.getHoldCount() + ")"); } finally { lock.unlock(); } } finally { lock.unlock(); } } }

try.expect: On the one-thread view, all three read balance lines print before any write balance: each credit suspended in the middle and let the next one in. With the Mutex, each credit reads and writes before the next one starts. The nested withLock times out after 500 ms, because a Mutex is not reentrant: the inner lock waits for the outer one, which waits for the inner one. The Java twin interleaves the same way on one thread, and its ReentrantLock reports a hold count of 2.

sections.h: Virtual time: runTest skips the delays
sections.html:
Testing coroutine code in real time is slow and flaky. A retry with waits of 100, 200 and 400 ms costs 700 ms per test, and a loaded CI machine turns 700 into 1,500 and your timing assertion into a coin toss. runTest from kotlinx-coroutines-test replaces the clock. Every delay in the test's coroutines is skipped, and a virtual clock jumps forward instead, keeping the order the delays would have produced.

Java
// Java equivalent: Reactor's StepVerifier with virtual time (reactor-test)
@Test
void waitsBetweenAttempts() {
    StepVerifier.withVirtualTime(() -> issuer.authorize(req)
            .retryWhen(Retry.backoff(2, Duration.ofMillis(100)).jitter(0)))
        .expectSubscription()
        .thenAwait(Duration.ofMillis(300))
        .expectNext(Decision.APPROVED)
        .verifyComplete();
}
Kotlin
@Test
fun `waits 100 then 200 ms between attempts`() = runTest {
    val attempts = mutableListOf<Long>()
    retryWithBackoff(times = 3, initialDelay = 100.milliseconds, maxDelay = 1.seconds) {
        attempts += currentTime                          // virtual milliseconds
        if (attempts.size < 3) throw IOException("issuer 503") else "ok"
    }
    assertThat(attempts).containsExactly(0L, 100L, 300L)  // in a few real milliseconds
}

runTest runs the body in a TestScope on a single-threaded test dispatcher, and currentTime reads the virtual clock. You can also drive the clock by hand: advanceTimeBy(ms) runs everything due before that point, runCurrent() runs what is due now, and advanceUntilIdle() runs everything queued. At the end, runTest waits for every child coroutine, so a test can't pass with work still pending.

Three rules keep the clock honest.

Only the test dispatcher's delays are virtual. Code that switches to Dispatchers.IO or Dispatchers.Default runs its delays in real time, and the test clock never sees them. That is why lesson 4 of this track injected the dispatchers: tests pass StandardTestDispatcher(testScheduler), production passes the real ones.

withTimeout inside runTest uses virtual time too. Combine it with real work on another dispatcher, and the scheduler, finding nothing of its own to do, can jump the clock forward and fire the timeout while the real work is still running. The lab tests in lesson 5 of this track use runBlocking for their blocking lookup for exactly that reason.

The runTest timeout is wall-clock time: 60 seconds by default since kotlinx.coroutines 1.8 (it was 10 s in 1.7). Change it with runTest(timeout = 10.seconds) or the kotlinx.coroutines.test.default_timeout system property. In 1.11 the old dispatchTimeoutMs overloads are errors.

try.title: Run five seconds of work in a blink
steps: Read VirtualTime.kt. It calls runTest from a plain main. Predict the virtual time of each log line, and how much real time the first runTest takes.
Look at the last line: why did the clock stay at 0 while a real second went by?

code.title: VirtualTime.kt
code.html: package workbench.coroutines.l10 import kotlinx.coroutines.Dispatchers import kotlinx.coroutines.ExperimentalCoroutinesApi import kotlinx.coroutines.async import kotlinx.coroutines.delay import kotlinx.coroutines.launch import kotlinx.coroutines.test.TestScope import kotlinx.coroutines.test.currentTime import kotlinx.coroutines.test.runTest import kotlinx.coroutines.withContext @OptIn(ExperimentalCoroutinesApi::class) fun main() { val realStart = System.nanoTime() fun real() = (System.nanoTime() - realStart) / 1_000_000 // runTest is meant for tests, but a plain main can call it too runTest { fun TestScope.log(what: String) = println("virtual %5d ms (real %4d ms) %s".format(currentTime, real(), what)) launch { delay(1_000); log("settlement file fetched") delay(200); log("file parsed") delay(2_000); log("ledger posted") } val fx = async { delay(3_000); log("FX rates fetched") delay(500); log("rates cached") } fx.await() log("await returned") } println("whole runTest took %d ms of real time".format(real())) runTest { val before = real() withContext(Dispatchers.Default) { delay(1_000) } // escapes the test scheduler println("withContext(Default) { delay(1_000) }: virtual $currentTime ms, real ${real() - before} ms") } }

try.expect: The lines print at virtual 1,000, 1,200, 3,000, 3,200 and 3,500 ms, in that order, and await returned at 3,500. The real time stays well under a second, and most of it is the test library starting up. The last runTest reports virtual 0 ms and about 1,000 real ms: withContext(Dispatchers.Default) left the test scheduler, so its delay was a real one.

sections.h: Standard or Unconfined, and backgroundScope for work that never ends
sections.html:
runTest uses a StandardTestDispatcher by default. With it, launch only queues the new coroutine, and nothing runs until the test body suspends or advances the scheduler. Tests stay predictable, because you decide when each child runs. Production dispatchers don't run a child immediately either, so this is also the more honest default.

UnconfinedTestDispatcher(testScheduler) enters a new coroutine at once and runs it to its first suspension, like Dispatchers.Unconfined. That is handy for a collector that must be subscribed before the next line emits, such as a test of a SharedFlow with no replay:

Java
// Java equivalent: StepVerifier subscribes first, then runs the action that emits
StepVerifier.create(tracker.transitions())
    .then(() -> tracker.moveTo(PaymentStatus.CAPTURED))
    .expectNextMatches(t -> t.to() == PaymentStatus.CAPTURED)
    .thenCancel()
    .verify();
Kotlin
backgroundScope.launch(UnconfinedTestDispatcher(testScheduler)) {
    tracker.transitions.collect { seen += it }    // subscribed before the next line runs
}
tracker.moveTo(PaymentStatus.CAPTURED)

If you mix dispatchers, give them all the same testScheduler. Two schedulers mean two clocks, and one of them will not move.

backgroundScope is for coroutines that never finish on their own: a poller, a collector of a StateFlow, the sharing scope of a stateIn. runTest waits for every child before it returns, so an endless child in the test scope itself would hang until the 60-second timeout. Coroutines in backgroundScope are cancelled when the test body ends instead. Two details matter. advanceUntilIdle() stops once only background work is left (otherwise a poller would keep it busy forever), so drive background work with advanceTimeBy. And a failure in backgroundScope doesn't stop the test at once, but it is reported when the test ends, so the test still fails.

This lesson's lab is written the way these rules suggest. The retry tests read currentTime to check each wait exactly, and the balance tests count how many conversions overlap instead of timing them. On the stub, one of those tests reports 0 virtual milliseconds: the stub's conversions ran on a real Default thread, outside the virtual clock.

For flows there is also Turbine (app.cash.turbine, not on this lab's classpath), which adds flow.test { awaitItem() }. Its waits use a 3-second wall-clock timeout, not the virtual clock.

try.title: Watch the two test dispatchers and a background poller
steps: Read TestDispatchers.kt. Predict the order in each of the two lists, and the poll count after each line.
Move the poller from backgroundScope.launch to a plain launch, and add runTest(timeout = 3.seconds) (import kotlin.time.Duration.Companion.seconds). Predict, then run.

code.title: TestDispatchers.kt
code.html: package workbench.coroutines.l10 import kotlinx.coroutines.ExperimentalCoroutinesApi import kotlinx.coroutines.delay import kotlinx.coroutines.launch import kotlinx.coroutines.test.UnconfinedTestDispatcher import kotlinx.coroutines.test.advanceTimeBy import kotlinx.coroutines.test.advanceUntilIdle import kotlinx.coroutines.test.runCurrent import kotlinx.coroutines.test.runTest @OptIn(ExperimentalCoroutinesApi::class) fun main() = runTest { // 1. runTest's default, StandardTestDispatcher: launch only queues the child val standard = mutableListOf<String>() launch { standard += "child ran" } standard += "after launch" runCurrent() // run what is due now println("StandardTestDispatcher: $standard") // 2. UnconfinedTestDispatcher: the child starts at once, up to its first suspension val unconfined = mutableListOf<String>() launch(UnconfinedTestDispatcher(testScheduler)) { unconfined += "child ran" } unconfined += "after launch" println("UnconfinedTestDispatcher: $unconfined") // 3. backgroundScope: for work that never ends, such as a rate poller var polls = 0 backgroundScope.launch { while (true) { delay(1_000); polls++ } } advanceTimeBy(5_500) println("polls after advanceTimeBy(5_500): $polls") advanceUntilIdle() println("polls after advanceUntilIdle(): $polls (background work doesn't keep it busy)") // when the test body ends, runTest cancels everything in backgroundScope }

try.expect: StandardTestDispatcher: [after launch, child ran] and UnconfinedTestDispatcher: [child ran, after launch]. The poller has run 5 times after advanceTimeBy(5_500), and still 5 after advanceUntilIdle(), which ignores background work. After your change, advanceUntilIdle() treats the poller as foreground work and runs it again and again, millions of virtual seconds' worth, until the 3-second wall-clock timeout stops everything with UncompletedCoroutinesError (an AssertionError): the test body did not run to completion.

analogy: Shared state is the cash drawer at a shop. An atomic is a till that adds a sale in one press of a key. A Mutex is the key to the drawer: whoever holds it counts, takes and writes down, and the others wait their turn, without standing around blocking the aisle (they suspend). A one-thread view is a rule that only one cashier stands at the till at a time. That rule doesn't stop a cashier from walking off to phone the bank in the middle of counting, letting the next cashier count the same drawer. runTest is a rehearsal with a stage clock that jumps straight to the next cue, so a day of trading takes seconds. The analogy breaks on reentry: a shopkeeper holding the drawer key can open the drawer twice. A coroutine holding a Mutex that asks for it again waits for itself forever.
world: Most payment state lives in Oracle, where row locks and unique keys do this job, but services keep some state in memory: per-merchant rate-limit counters, a cache of FX rates, the in-flight totals of a settlement run. Counters belong in atomics. A compound update, such as checking a merchant's daily limit and then reserving the amount, needs a Mutex held across the check and the reservation, with any suspending call (the FX conversion, the fraud score) done before the lock if you can. Don't reach for limitedParallelism(1) as a lock: it serializes code only between suspension points. For tests, inject dispatchers everywhere (Quarkus beans can take a CoroutineDispatcher from a producer method), so a test passes StandardTestDispatcher(testScheduler) and a retry policy with a 30-second cap tests in milliseconds.
mistake: The most common mistake is protecting a sequence that suspends in the middle with something that only works between suspensions: a limitedParallelism(1) view, a single-threaded dispatcher, or synchronized around code that was refactored into a suspend function. It passes code review because it reads like a lock, and it passes tests that never make two coroutines overlap. Under load, two credits read the same balance, both suspend in the FX call, and one overwrites the other. The fix is to look for every suspension point inside the critical section. Move it out (compute first, then read and write with nothing in between), or hold a Mutex across the whole sequence and keep that sequence short.

compare.title: A merchant limit check: ReentrantLock vs Mutex

java.title: DailyLimits.java
java.html: class DailyLimits { private final Map<String, Long> spent = new HashMap<>(); private final ReentrantLock lock = new ReentrantLock(); boolean reserve(String merchant, long cents, long limit) { long risk = fraud.score(merchant, cents); // 1. the slow call, outside the lock (blocks a thread) lock.lock(); // 2. blocks the thread while waiting try { long already = spent.getOrDefault(merchant, 0L); if (risk > 80 || already + cents > limit) return false; spent.put(merchant, already + cents); // 3. check and reserve together return true; } finally { lock.unlock(); } } }

kotlin.title: DailyLimits.kt
kotlin.html: class DailyLimits { private val spent = HashMap<String, Long>() private val mutex = Mutex() suspend fun reserve(merchant: String, cents: Long, limit: Long): Boolean { val risk = fraud.score(merchant, cents) // 1. the slow call, outside the lock (suspends) return mutex.withLock { // 2. suspends while waiting, holds no thread val already = spent[merchant] ?: 0L if (risk > 80 || already + cents > limit) return@withLock false spent[merchant] = already + cents // 3. check and reserve together true } } }

compare.note: The shape is identical: do the slow call first, then check and reserve under one lock. Two things differ. Waiting for a ReentrantLock blocks a thread, while waiting for a Mutex suspends a coroutine, so a burst of 5,000 reservations doesn't need 5,000 threads. And the Java lock is reentrant while the Mutex isn't, so a helper that takes the Mutex again from inside withLock hangs instead of nesting. The Kotlin version has one extra trap that Java can't have: if someone later moves fraud.score inside withLock, it still works but holds the lock across a network call, and if they replace the Mutex with a one-thread dispatcher, it stops being correct at all.

worked.title: Test a retry policy without waiting for it

steps.say: A capture client retries the issuer on IOException: up to 5 attempts, waits starting at 200 ms, doubling, capped at 2 s. The existing test uses real time and Thread.sleep. It takes 3 seconds, and it fails on CI about once a week.
steps.code: @Test fun `retries on 503`() = runBlocking { var calls = 0 val started = System.currentTimeMillis() val result = client.captureWithRetry(cmd) { calls++; if (calls < 4) throw IOException("503") else "ok" } assertThat(result).isEqualTo("ok") assertThat(System.currentTimeMillis() - started).isBetween(1_350L, 1_600L) // 200 + 400 + 800 = 1,400 }

alt.html: // Java equivalent of the flaky test: real sleeps, a timing window @Test void retriesOn503() { AtomicInteger calls = new AtomicInteger(); long started = System.currentTimeMillis(); String result = client.captureWithRetry(cmd, () -> { if (calls.incrementAndGet() < 4) throw new UncheckedIOException(new IOException("503")); return "ok"; }); assertThat(result).isEqualTo("ok"); assertThat(System.currentTimeMillis() - started).isBetween(1_350L, 1_600L); }

steps.say: Move to runTest. The waits are delay calls on the test dispatcher, so they become virtual, and the test can check each attempt's exact virtual time instead of a window.
steps.code: @Test fun `waits 200, 400, then 800 ms between attempts`() = runTest { val at = mutableListOf<Long>() val result = client.captureWithRetry(cmd) { at += currentTime // 1. record virtual ms per attempt if (at.size < 4) throw IOException("503") else "ok" } assertThat(result).isEqualTo("ok") assertThat(at).containsExactly(0L, 200L, 600L, 1_400L) // 2. exact, and instant }

alt.html: // Java equivalent: Reactor's virtual time, if the client is built on Reactor @Test void waitsBetweenAttempts() { StepVerifier.withVirtualTime(() -> client.captureWithRetry(cmd)) .expectSubscription() .thenAwait(Duration.ofMillis(1_400)) // 1. advance the virtual clock .expectNext("ok") // 2. exact, and instant .verifyComplete(); }

steps.say: The test went back to real time when someone added withContext(Dispatchers.IO) around the HTTP call inside the client: its delay calls now ran on IO. Inject the dispatcher, and give the test the test scheduler's one.
steps.code: class CaptureClient(private val io: CoroutineDispatcher = Dispatchers.IO) { suspend fun <T> captureWithRetry(cmd: Capture, call: suspend () -> T): T = withContext(io) { retryWithBackoff(times = 5, initialDelay = 200.milliseconds, maxDelay = 2.seconds) { call() } } } // 3. in the test val client = CaptureClient(io = StandardTestDispatcher(testScheduler))

alt.html: // Java equivalent: inject the Scheduler, and give the test a virtual one class CaptureClient { private final Scheduler io; CaptureClient(Scheduler io) { this.io = io; } <T> Mono<T> captureWithRetry(Capture cmd, Mono<T> call) { return call.subscribeOn(io) .retryWhen(Retry.backoff(4, Duration.ofMillis(200)).maxBackoff(Duration.ofSeconds(2)).jitter(0).scheduler(io)); } } // 3. in the test VirtualTimeScheduler vts = VirtualTimeScheduler.getOrSet(); CaptureClient client = new CaptureClient(vts);

steps.say: Add the case people forget: cancellation during a wait must stop the retries. Virtual time lets you stop exactly between two attempts.
steps.code: @Test fun `a cancel during the backoff stops the retries`() = runTest { var calls = 0 val job = launch { client.captureWithRetry(cmd) { calls++; throw IOException("503") } } advanceTimeBy(300) // 4. attempts at 0 and 200 ms; now waiting until 600 ms job.cancel() advanceUntilIdle() assertThat(calls).isEqualTo(2) }

alt.html: @Test void cancelDuringBackoffStopsRetries() { AtomicInteger calls = new AtomicInteger(); StepVerifier.withVirtualTime(() -> client.captureWithRetry(cmd, Mono.<String>fromCallable(() -> { calls.incrementAndGet(); throw new IOException("503"); }))) .expectSubscription() .thenAwait(Duration.ofMillis(300)) // 4. attempts at 0 and 200 ms .thenCancel() .verify(); assertThat(calls.get()).isEqualTo(2); }

steps.say: Self-check: suppose the helper wrapped both the attempt and the delay in one runCatching and retried on any failure. What would the cancel test report? (calls would be 5, not 2. After the cancel, each delay throws at once, runCatching swallows it as a failed attempt, and the loop races through the remaining attempts. The test catches it because it counts calls instead of timing them. Lesson 5 of this track showed the same trap.)

lab.title: Fix a balance book, then write retry with backoff
steps: Run the tests. All seven fail. Read SharedStateAndTestingTest.kt first: it is the spec, and every test runs on virtual time.
In BalanceBook.credit, call fx.toEurCents first, outside any lock. Then do the read and the write inside mutex.withLock { }. Replace the one-thread view with a Mutex in balance too.

Write retryWithBackoff. Loop over attempts 1 to times - 1: return the block's result on success; on an exception, rethrow CancellationException, rethrow when retryOn is false, otherwise delay and grow the wait. Then make the last attempt outside the loop, so its exception reaches the caller.
Run the tests until all seven pass.
hints: On the stub, 100 concurrent credits all land reports 100 cents instead of 10,000: every credit read 0 before any wrote. The second test reports 0 virtual ms because the stub's conversions ran on a real Default thread, outside the test clock.
Catch CancellationException before Exception, and rethrow it. kotlin.coroutines.cancellation.CancellationException is the class to import.
The cancel test cancels the job during a delay. A delay that is not inside your try simply throws, and the loop ends without another attempt.

drill.title: A safe counter map and a virtual-time test, from memory
drill.prompt: Close this page. Write class MerchantCounts with suspend fun record(merchant: String) that calls a suspending fraud.check(merchant) first, then increments that merchant's count, safe for many coroutines on Dispatchers.Default. Then write a runTest test that checks a function pollEvery(1.seconds) has polled 3 times after 3.5 virtual seconds, using backgroundScope for the endless poller.

answer.html: class MerchantCounts(private val fraud: FraudCheck) { private val counts = HashMap<String, Int>() private val mutex = Mutex() suspend fun record(merchant: String) { fraud.check(merchant) // suspends: keep it outside the lock mutex.withLock { counts[merchant] = (counts[merchant] ?: 0) + 1 } } } @Test fun `polls once a second`() = runTest { var polls = 0 backgroundScope.launch { pollEvery(1.seconds) { polls++ } } // never ends on its own advanceTimeBy(3_500) assertThat(polls).isEqualTo(3) }

alt.title: Java equivalent
alt.html: // Java equivalent: a lock-free counter map, and Reactor virtual time for the poller class MerchantCounts { private final ConcurrentHashMap<String, Integer> counts = new ConcurrentHashMap<>(); void record(String merchant) { fraud.check(merchant); // blocking: outside any lock counts.merge(merchant, 1, Integer::sum); // one atomic step } } @Test void pollsOnceASecond() { StepVerifier.withVirtualTime(() -> Flux.interval(Duration.ofSeconds(1)).map(tick -> poll())) .expectSubscription() .thenAwait(Duration.ofMillis(3_500)) .expectNextCount(3) .thenCancel() .verify(); }

recap: Coroutines on Dispatchers.Default race like threads. @Volatile doesn't make count++ safe; atomics do, for single values.
A Mutex protects a sequence of steps. withLock suspends instead of blocking, and the Mutex is fair and not reentrant: locking it again from inside hangs.
limitedParallelism(1) serializes code only between suspension points, so a read, a suspending call and a write on it can lose updates. Move the suspension out, or hold a Mutex.
runTest skips delay with a virtual clock (currentTime, advanceTimeBy, runCurrent, advanceUntilIdle). Delays on real dispatchers stay real, so inject dispatchers.
StandardTestDispatcher (the default) queues new coroutines; UnconfinedTestDispatcher starts them at once. Share one testScheduler between them.
Put never-ending coroutines in backgroundScope. advanceUntilIdle ignores them, and runTest cancels them at the end.

explain.prompt: A teammate replaced a Mutex with Dispatchers.Default.limitedParallelism(1) in the merchant limit check "because it's simpler and only one coroutine runs at a time anyway". The check calls the fraud service between reading and writing the limit. Explain what can go wrong, and how you'd test it without real time.
explain.answer: The one-thread view only guarantees one coroutine at a time between suspension points. The fraud call suspends, so while one check waits for the fraud service, the thread runs the next check, which reads the same "spent so far" value. Both then pass the limit check and both reserve, so a merchant can go over its limit. A Mutex held across the whole check keeps the second one out even while the first is suspended; better still, call the fraud service first and then do the read and the reservation together under the lock, with nothing suspending in between. To test it, I'd use runTest with a fake fraud service that just calls delay(50), launch a hundred reservations, and assert on the totals and on how many overlapped. On virtual time that is deterministic and runs in milliseconds, as long as the class takes its dispatcher as a parameter instead of hard-coding Dispatchers.Default.

deeper.html:
Semaphore(permits) in kotlinx.coroutines.sync is the counting version of a Mutex: withPermit { } lets at most n coroutines in at once. It is the coroutine counterpart of the shared Semaphore from lesson 3 of the virtual threads track, and like the Mutex it suspends rather than blocks. Since 1.9 you can no longer cast a Mutex to a Semaphore; they are separate types.

Mutex has an optional owner: lock(owner) and withLock(owner) record who holds it, and holdsLock(owner) checks it. Passing an owner turns a reentrant call into an immediate IllegalStateException instead of a silent hang, which is a cheap safety net in code where a helper might be called with the lock held.

The test library has more knobs than this lesson uses. Several StandardTestDispatcher(testScheduler, name = ...) instances can share one scheduler, so production code that takes two dispatchers (IO and CPU) can get two named test dispatchers with one clock. Dispatchers.setMain(...) and resetMain() swap the Main dispatcher for UI-style code. And runTest reports uncaught exceptions from coroutines it doesn't own at the end of the test, through a ServiceLoader hook, which is why a forgotten GlobalScope.launch that throws can fail an unrelated test.

Finally, virtual time is not a load test. It proves that the order and the timing logic are right. It says nothing about how long the real FX service takes, how a real Mutex behaves with 5,000 waiters, or whether Oracle keeps up. Keep a few real-time integration tests, with generous margins, for that.
